newsitem.title: UK: CBOT-LIFFE wheat talks on hold until T-bond link.
newsitem.headline: CBOT-LIFFE wheat talks on hold until T-bond link.

text.p: The Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) and the London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE) have shelved plans for a link on wheat futures possibly until spring 1997, a CBOT official said on Tuesday.

Jeff Campbell, CBOT's senior product manager, said on the fringes of a London conference that talks could resume once a trade linkage between the two exchanges on Treasury bonds, now postponed to May 1997, came into effect.

"Right now it's on hold. It's been on hold since LIFFE started merger talks with the LCE (London Commodity Exchange)," Campbell told Reuters during a two-day conference on Risk Management in Agriculture.

Before its merger with LIFFE in September, the LCE looked at a joint venture with the CBOT to trade grain in London. But now officials say the new wheat contract, in whatever form, is unlikely to start trading before 1998.

The two most likely options considered are launching a new European wheat contract, or simply listing the existing benchmark CBOT wheat and other agricultural contracts in London to capture the European time zone.

Traders say a new contract is unnecessary given that two new wheat contracts in Amsterdam and in Paris are struggling for survival. This is because the farming sector in the European Union (EU) has very little exposure to world price risks and relies on government subsidies.
LIFFE is also considering extending the delivery of its existing feed wheat contract to encompass European ports.

It says prices of feed wheat and the European physical benchmark of Rouen-delivered milling wheat move in tandem and the London market could become a good hedge for European players if local delivery was introduced.

Clive Furness, director of commodity products at LIFFE, said that despite the apparent failure of the Amsterdam and Paris launches, LIFFE was not eliminating the possibility of developing a new wheat contract to win the title of a European benchmark.
"We have to look carefully to what exchange links can do for us. I don't know where this is going to take us," Furness told the conference.

The CBOT's Campbell said although the odds were against any new contract -- the CBOT is also suffering lack of turnover for its new crop yield futures -- a joint wheat deal would enable LIFFE to have access to the CBOT's large pool of investors.
The CBOT in turn sees potential in Europe as governments are forced to bring subsidies down under world trade agreements and farmers are left to their own devices to manage risks.
"We think that as EU and other countries are more exposed and less protected, the correlation between our prices (CBOT) and local prices will become much stronger," said Campbell.
